l: death plot against Achilles’ son, Hecuba and other plays, THE NURSE OF HERMIONE, CHORUS.
s: Orestes says that he has arranged an unavoidable death plot against Achilles’ son with armed allies stationed in the Pythian realm. He intends to present the deed as an exploit at Delphi and claims that Apollo will bring vengeance upon Achilles’ son.

l: Hermione’s marriage, Hecuba and other plays, THE NURSE OF HERMIONE, CHORUS.
s: Orestes says that Hermione’s father first betrothed her to Orestes and later promised her to Achilles’ son if Troy were conquered. Achilles’ son then married Hermione after returning from Troy, while also loving Andromache, whom Hermione calls a captive rival.

l: Hecuba and other plays, Hecuba and other plays, PELEUS, CHORUS.
s: Peleus learns from the Chorus and a Messenger that Hermione has fled and that Achilles’ son has been killed by Orestes and Delphi’s citizens at Apollo’s temple. The Messenger describes how Achilles’ son resisted the ambush before being overwhelmed, and his body is brought back to Peleus. Thetis appears, orders that the body be buried at Delphi, assigns Andromache to Helenus in Molossia with her young son, and promises to make Peleus immortal. Peleus accepts her commands, while the Chorus concludes that the gods bring unexpected outcomes through fate.

l: Peleus, Hecuba and other plays, PELEUS, CHORUS.
s: Peleus learns that Hermione has fled and that Achilles’ son has been killed at Delphi. He mourns the loss of his grandson and laments that he is left childless, but Thetis consoles him, commands him to bury the body, and promises to make him immortal.

l: Chorus of Phthian women, Hecuba and other plays, PELEUS, CHORUS.
s: The Chorus tells Peleus that Hermione has fled because of Menelaus’ anger and that Orestes intends to kill Achilles’ son. It mourns the dead youth and Peleus’s suffering, then recognizes the arrival of Thetis and concludes that the gods guide human affairs in unexpected ways.

l: Messenger, Hecuba and other plays, PELEUS, CHORUS.
s: The Messenger reports that Achilles’ son was killed by Delphi’s citizens and Orestes. He describes the ambush at Apollo’s temple, Achilles’ son’s resistance, his eventual slaughter, and the return of his body to Peleus.

l: Thetis, Hecuba and other plays, PELEUS, CHORUS.
s: Thetis appears from the house of Nereus and counsels Peleus not to despair. She orders Achilles’ son’s body taken to Delphi for burial, directs Andromache and her young son to Molossia, and promises to make Peleus immortal.

l: Neoptolemus, Hecuba and other plays, PELEUS, CHORUS.
s: Achilles’ son is lured to Apollo’s temple at Delphi by Orestes’ accusations and is attacked by Delphi’s citizens. He fights bravely but is overwhelmed, killed, mutilated, and carried back to Peleus for burial.

l: Orestes, Hecuba and other plays, PELEUS, CHORUS.
s: Orestes spreads accusations that Achilles’ son intends to overthrow Apollo’s temple and organizes the attack against him. He is identified as the stranger from Mycenae who helped bring about Achilles’ son’s death.

l: Hermione, Hecuba and other plays, PELEUS, CHORUS.
s: Hermione flees Peleus’s house because she fears that her lord will cast her out after she plotted to kill the boy. Peleus later curses the marriage that brought her into his house and calls her an execrable fiend.

l: Andromache, Hecuba and other plays, PELEUS, CHORUS.
s: Thetis directs Andromache to marry Helenus and live in Molossia. Through her, the remaining royal line connected with Aeacus will continue.

l: Andromache’s young son, Hecuba and other plays, PELEUS, CHORUS.
s: Andromache’s young son is described by Thetis as the only remaining royal branch of the stem of Aeacus. He is to live with Andromache in Molossia, where his descendants will rule.

l: Achilles, Hecuba and other plays, PELEUS, CHORUS.
s: Achilles is remembered as the son of Thetis and the first of the Greek heroes. Thetis says that he dwells in an island washed by the Euxine and that Peleus will behold him there after becoming immortal.

l: Apollo, Hecuba and other plays, PELEUS, CHORUS.
s: Apollo’s temple is the setting of Achilles’ son’s killing. The Messenger says that Apollo has avenged himself on Achilles’ son, while also questioning how a god who prophesies and dispenses justice can act like a worthless human enemy.

l: Delphi, Hecuba and other plays, PELEUS, CHORUS.
s: Delphi is the sacred realm and city where Achilles’ son is ambushed and killed. Thetis commands Peleus to return the body there so that its tomb will proclaim the violence committed by Orestes’ band.

l: Delphi’s citizens, Hecuba and other plays, PELEUS, CHORUS.
s: Delphi’s citizens are persuaded by Orestes’ accusations that Achilles’ son intends to attack Apollo’s temple. They ambush him, hurl stones and weapons, and finally kill him in great numbers.

l: Phthia, Hecuba and other plays, PELEUS, CHORUS.
s: Phthia is Peleus’s city and the location of his house. Peleus laments that he has no children or descendants left to occupy its mansions.

l: Molossia, Hecuba and other plays, PELEUS, CHORUS.
s: Molossia is the land where Thetis orders Andromache and her young son to live. The young son’s descendants are destined to rule there as a succession of happy kings.

l: Pelion, Hecuba and other plays, PELEUS, CHORUS.
s: Peleus says he will go to the cave of Pelion after burying his grandson. It is associated with the place where he first received Thetis in his arms.

l: Sepia cave, Hecuba and other plays, PELEUS, CHORUS.
s: Thetis tells Peleus to keep his station in the cave that time has worn through the rock of Sepia. She will later come with the Nereids to carry him away.

l: Apollo’s temple at Delphi, Hecuba and other plays, PELEUS, CHORUS.
s: Apollo’s temple at Delphi is where Orestes arranges the ambush against Achilles’ son. Achilles’ son initially seeks to make atonement there, but Delphi’s citizens attack and kill him beside the altar.

l: Neoptolemus’s murder at Delphi, Hecuba and other plays, PELEUS, CHORUS.
s: The murder of Achilles’ son at Delphi is carried out by a Delphian with the help of a multitude after Orestes has turned the citizens against him. His body is covered with wounds and cast from the temple before being taken to Peleus.

l: Neoptolemus’s burial, Hecuba and other plays, PELEUS, CHORUS.
s: Thetis orders Achilles’ son’s body to be taken back to Delphi and buried there. His tomb is to testify to the murderous violence committed by Orestes’ band.

l: Peleus’s apotheosis, Hecuba and other plays, PELEUS, CHORUS.
s: Thetis promises to release Peleus from human suffering by making him immortal and incorruptible. He will live with her as a god in Nereus’s watery dwelling and later behold Achilles.

l: marriage of Thetis and Peleus, Hecuba and other plays, PELEUS, CHORUS.
s: Thetis recalls the ties of her marriage with Peleus and presents his having married a goddess as a blessing. Peleus says that a prudent man should choose a nobly born consort and marry his daughters into virtuous families rather than rely on wealth.

l: Fortune, Hecuba and other plays, PELEUS, CHORUS.
s: Thetis says that Peleus must endure the suffering imposed by fate because Zeus has ordained it, and that death is a debt owed by all humanity. The Chorus concludes that the gods often bring about what mortals least expect while still guiding events through life’s perplexity.

l: Medea, Medea, INTRODUCTION
s: The introduction presents Euripides’ Medea as a tragedy of character and situation about the collapse of Jason and Medea’s relationship rather than as a romantic adventure. It recounts how Medea, princess and enchantress of Colchis, aided Jason and the Argonauts, abandoned her family, and followed Jason to Greece, where he later accepted a Corinthian princess’s hand. The play begins when Jason’s betrayal leads Creon to condemn Medea to exile, and it develops into a study of oppression, revenge, and the destructive transformation of suffering into hatred. The introduction emphasizes the play’s intense dramatic power, its early originality, and its deliberately unsettling refusal to offer moral consolation.

l: Medea (play), Medea, INTRODUCTION
s: The Medea is described as a tragedy of character and situation rather than a romantic play. It focuses on the aftermath of Jason and Medea’s romance, presenting an intensely passionate study of oppression and revenge in which Medea becomes the instrument of judgment against Jason.

l: Medea, Medea, INTRODUCTION
s: Medea is the princess and enchantress of Colchis who falls in love with Jason, helps him complete his quest, kills her own brother Absyrtus, and abandons her home to follow him. After Jason accepts a Corinthian princess and Medea is condemned to exile, her devotion turns into hatred; the introduction portrays her as a wronged woman transformed into a living Curse.

l: Jason, Medea, INTRODUCTION
s: Jason is the son of Aeson and a famous Argonaut who seeks the Golden Ram’s fleece and his ancestral honour. He accepts Medea’s help and flight from Colchis, but later abandons her for a Corinthian marriage in pursuit of political security and a great career; the introduction presents him as ambitious, calculating, and fundamentally unchanged from his heroic past.

l: Euripides, Medea, INTRODUCTION
s: Euripides is presented as a poet who uses the Medea to expose the tragedy beneath heroic romance and to examine how cruelty damages both its victim and the eventual avenger. His treatment is described as youthful, austere, passionate, skeptical, and intensely realistic, while still allowing poetry to break through at moments of greatest emotional force.

l: Colchis, Medea, INTRODUCTION
s: Colchis is the distant land ruled by Aietes and the destination of Jason’s quest for the Golden Ram’s fleece and the soul of Phrixus. It is Medea’s homeland, which she betrays and leaves when she helps Jason escape.

l: Corinth, Medea, INTRODUCTION
s: Corinth is the place to which Jason directs his flight with Medea after the catastrophe at Iolcos. It is governed by Creon, whose daughter Jason marries, and it becomes the setting in which Medea is treated as a dangerous foreigner and condemned to exile.

l: Argo, Medea, INTRODUCTION
s: The Argo is the first ship, built for Jason’s expedition to Colchis. The introduction notes that Jason’s love for the ship may be the clearest surviving flash of his heroic and romantic past.

l: the Argonauts, Medea, INTRODUCTION
s: The Argonauts are the daring heroes gathered from across Hellas to accompany Jason on the quest. Medea helps them survive their journey and serves as a constant helper and counsellor during the voyage home.

l: the Argo legend, Medea, INTRODUCTION
s: The Argo legend is described as wild and beautiful and as running through Greek literature from early Corinthian lays to Pindar and Apollonius Rhodius. Euripides draws on this legendary material but looks past its enchantment to the tragedy beneath it.

l: romance, Medea, INTRODUCTION
s: The romance between Jason and Medea is treated as something whose ending is the reverse of its earlier enchantment. The introduction argues that most romances contain a flaw, and that the flaw in this one is fatal because Jason’s ambition and Medea’s destructive devotion make their relationship incapable of lasting.

l: tragedy, Medea, INTRODUCTION
s: The tragedy of Medea is rooted in the collision between Jason’s pursuit of status and Medea’s betrayed love. Its dramatic power comes from showing oppression turning the victim into an agent of further cruelty rather than into a figure of morally triumphant virtue.

l: love, Medea, INTRODUCTION
s: Medea’s love for Jason leads her to help him, kill for him, abandon her family, and expect a perfect love in return. When Jason rejects her, that love becomes hatred, revealing the introduction’s view that her devotion had always contained a potentially ugly and destructive intensity.

l: oppression and revenge, Medea, INTRODUCTION
s: Oppression and revenge form a recurring Euripidean dramatic pattern discussed in the introduction. Euripides shows that cruelty not only causes suffering but can make the victim worse, so the eventual revenge no longer appears as a triumph of justice.

l: vengeance, Medea, INTRODUCTION
s: Revenge in the Medea is presented as powerful but morally and emotionally unsatisfying. Medea’s injuries give her superhuman force, yet her punishment of Jason comes through a victim transformed into something like a devil, leaving the audience longing for explanation, forgiveness, or consolation.

l: Medea, Medea, MEDEA
s: The Nurse and the Attendant describe Medea's grief after Jason abandons her to marry Creon's daughter, and they fear that her anger may lead to violence. Medea emerges and explains to the Corinthian women the hardships of marriage, exile, and dependence on a husband, asking them not to betray her if she finds a way to punish Jason. Creon orders Medea and her two children to leave Corinth, but Medea persuades him to grant them one more day. Creon warns that Medea or either child will die if they remain after the following sunrise.

l: Medea, Medea, MEDEA
s: Medea is devastated because Jason has abandoned her to marry Creon's daughter. She curses Jason, his bride, and their house, and tells the Corinthian women that she may become dangerous if deprived of her rights in love. She persuades Creon to allow her and the children to remain for one more day.

l: Jason, Medea, MEDEA
s: Jason has forsaken Medea and his two sons in order to marry Creon's daughter and live in a king's chamber. The Nurse and the Attendant describe him as no longer acting like a husband or father, while Medea calls him evil and vows to repay his betrayal.

l: Creon, Medea, MEDEA
s: Creon orders Medea and her two children to leave Corinth because he fears that Medea will harm his daughter, Jason, or himself. Although he distrusts her, he grants her one day to remain, warning that she or either child will die if found in Corinth after the next sunrise.

l: the Nurse, Medea, MEDEA
s: The Nurse explains Medea's history with Jason and fears that Medea may kill herself, Jason, the bridegroom, or the king. She tries to keep the children away from Medea while Medea's anger is intense, and she asks the Chorus to understand Medea's suffering.

l: the two children of Jason and Medea, Medea, MEDEA
s: The two children return from playing unaware of their mother's distress, but the Nurse and the Attendant try to keep them apart from her. Creon's decree orders them into exile with Medea, and Creon later threatens that they will die if they remain in Corinth after the appointed day.

l: the Chorus of Corinthian Women, Medea, MEDEA
s: The Chorus comes after hearing Medea's cries and expresses sympathy for her suffering. Its members promise not to betray her when she asks for help, but they also fear that her grief may move against the innocent children.

l: Corinth, Medea, MEDEA
s: Corinth is the city where Medea lives with Jason and their children, and where Jason is to marry Creon's daughter. Creon commands Medea and the children to leave the city's borders.

l: Medea's house, Medea, MEDEA
s: Medea's house is the place where she lies fasting and grieving after Jason's betrayal. The Nurse fears that Medea may die there or use a blade against Jason, and Medea later comes out of the house to address the Corinthian women.

l: the oath between Medea and Jason, Medea, MEDEA
s: Medea recalls the oath, clasped hands, and vows that bound her and Jason together. She calls on Zeus and Themis to witness that Jason has broken faith and asks that the end of the oath be marked.

l: the marriage of Jason and Creon's daughter, Medea, MEDEA
s: Jason's planned marriage to Creon's daughter is the cause of Medea's abandonment and grief. Creon says that he is acting to protect his daughter, while Medea curses the bride and the house connected with the marriage.

l: Medea's exile, Medea, MEDEA
s: Creon declares that Medea and her two children must leave Corinth and not return. Medea accepts the exile but asks for one day to find counsel and comfort for the children.

l: Medea's revenge, Medea, MEDEA
s: Medea tells the Corinthian women that she seeks a way to requite Jason for his betrayal. She asks them not to reveal her intentions and declares that a woman deprived of her rights in love may become a bloodier spirit than anyone expects.

l: betrayal, Medea, MEDEA
s: Jason's abandonment of Medea is presented as a betrayal of their marriage, shared history, and oath. Medea describes herself as cast aside after leaving her father's home and land for Jason.

l: marriage and women's suffering, Medea, MEDEA
s: Medea says that women must pay for marriage, accept a master of their bodies, and learn how to live peacefully with a husband in unfamiliar laws and places. She argues that women remain bound to one person while men can leave home for other pleasures, and that bearing children is a greater burden than facing battle three times.

l: love, Medea, MEDEA
s: The Nurse says that human suffering is bound up with the way man and woman move together in love, but Jason's new love has weakened his old attachment. Medea says that Jason was once her whole world and that his betrayal has shattered her life.

l: Corinthian royal authority, Medea, MEDEA
s: Creon exercises Corinthian royal authority by ordering Medea and the children into exile and threatening them with death if they disobey. He describes the decree as his judgment and says that neither Medea's words nor her arts can overturn it.

l: Medea, Medea, MEDEA.
s: Medea, facing exile after Jason’s marriage to another bride, declares that the bride, her father, and Jason will die. She considers burning the house, stabbing the wedding pair, or using poison, while fearing that she will have nowhere to escape afterward. Medea invokes Hecate and resolves to act boldly, while the Chorus and the women lament her abandonment and suggest that women may become terrible and glorious in future stories.

l: Medea, Medea, MEDEA.
s: Medea believes that her defeat is not yet complete and plans revenge against Jason, the bride, and the bride's father. She considers several methods of murder, invokes Hecate for help, and urges herself to act boldly despite the danger and the possibility of having no refuge.

l: Jason, Medea, MEDEA.
s: Jason is identified by Medea as the man who gave the bride and as one of the three people she intends to kill. Medea says she once shaped her plans for his sake but now regards him as a thief whose marriage has brought about her exile.

l: Jason's new bride, Medea, MEDEA.
s: The bride is the woman who has been married to Jason and placed above Medea in the nearer house. Medea includes her among the three people who will die, and the Chorus describes her as queenlier and dearer in that household.

l: Creon, Medea, MEDEA.
s: The bride's father is included among the three people Medea intends to kill. He is also associated with the house from which Medea has been hunted away.

l: the Chorus of Corinthian Women, Medea, MEDEA.
s: The Chorus declares that life and its laws have changed and predicts that women will become terrible in story. It suggests that old accounts of women will be replaced and laments that men have long known and preserved stories of wrongs done to women.

l: the women of the Chorus, Medea, MEDEA.
s: The women sing of Medea's journey from her father's home across the sea and into a land where she has become an alien and landless ranger. They describe the weakening of the great oath and her loss of both her father's house and the household where she was once promised love.

l: the wedding, Medea, MEDEA.
s: Medea vows that the bride and groom's wedding feast and the day on which they joined hands will be dark. The wedding is presented as the event that accompanies Medea's rejection and expulsion.

l: Medea's exile, Medea, MEDEA.
s: Medea says that Jason has granted her one long day before exile, giving her time to act. She fears that after the murders no friend, land, or trustworthy door will shelter her from her enemies.

l: the planned murders, Medea, MEDEA.
s: Medea plans the deaths of Jason, the bride, and the bride's father. She debates burning their house, stabbing the married pair, or using poison, and she resolves to kill them even if she must then die herself.

l: marriage and gender relations, Medea, MEDEA.
s: Marriage is shown as a structure in which the new bride becomes more valued and Medea is displaced and hunted away. The Chorus argues that women may become powerful figures in story, while men may become fearful and low, reversing familiar accounts of gender.

l: Medea, Medea, _Enter from the right_ JASON.
s: Medea confronts Jason over his betrayal, reminding him that she rescued him and sacrificed her family and homeland for his sake, while Jason defends his remarriage as a way to secure prosperity and royal connections for himself and their children. Jason offers Medea aid for her exile, but she rejects it, and he leaves after blaming her curses and anger for her suffering. Aegeus, king of Athens, then meets Medea and reveals that he is childless; he swears to receive and protect her in Athens. Medea departs from the meeting with renewed confidence in the plan she intends to carry out before leaving Corinth.

l: Medea, Medea, _Enter from the right_ JASON.
s: Medea denounces Jason for abandoning her after she rescued him, betrayed her father, left her homeland, and helped destroy Pelias for his sake. She refuses Jason's offers of assistance, secures Aegeus's oath of protection in Athens, and leaves the encounter resolved to carry out her plan before departing.

l: Jason, Medea, _Enter from the right_ JASON.
s: Jason claims that Medea's angry speech and curses caused her exile, while he presents his marriage to another woman as a prudent effort to secure a prosperous royal household and future for his children. He offers Medea provisions, money, and recommendations to friends abroad, but she rejects his help.

l: Aegeus, Medea, _Enter from the right_ JASON.
s: Aegeus, king of Athens, meets Medea while returning from Delphi and agrees to receive and protect her in Athens. At her request, he swears by Earth, the Sun, and the gods never to cast her out or allow anyone else to seize her while he lives and is free.

l: Jason's new bride, Medea, _Enter from the right_ JASON.
s: Jason's new bride is described as the daughter of the ruler of Corinth and as the woman whom Jason has taken to rule his house. Medea curses the marriage and predicts that the bride may bring Jason suffering before he kisses her.

l: the two children of Jason and Medea, Medea, _Enter from the right_ JASON.
s: Jason says that he sought his new marriage partly to give Medea and their children security, to raise their sons in a manner worthy of his race, and to connect them with royal children. He offers aid for the children's exile, but Medea refuses it.

l: the Chorus of Corinthian Women, Medea, _Enter from the right_ JASON.
s: The Chorus judges the hatred between Medea and Jason to be terrible and beyond healing. It sings against destructive passion and laments the fate of a woman cast out from her home and left without a city, brother, or protector.

l: Corinth, Medea, _Enter from the right_ JASON.
s: Corinth is ruled by Creon, who has ordered Medea and her children into exile. Jason describes life in a Greek land such as Corinth as orderly and governed by justice and law, while Medea associates Corinth with her rejection and ruin.

l: Athens, Medea, _Enter from the right_ JASON.
s: Athens is the place where Aegeus promises Medea a home and protection. He says that once she reaches Attic earth, he will keep her safe and ensure that she cannot be seized again.

l: Medea's exile, Medea, _Enter from the right_ JASON.
s: Medea and her children are to be driven from Corinth without the security of their home. Jason offers provisions and assistance for their exile, but Medea refuses his gifts and instead obtains Aegeus's promise of refuge in Athens.

l: Jason's betrayal and remarriage, Medea, _Enter from the right_ JASON.
s: Jason has taken another wife, the daughter of the ruler of Corinth, after abandoning Medea despite her sacrifices and their children. He defends the remarriage as a way to gain prosperity, royal connections, and a stronger future for the children, while Medea calls it a violation of sworn faith.

l: Medea's rescue of Jason, Medea, _Enter from the right_ JASON.
s: Medea says that she saved Jason by helping him yoke the fiery bulls, sow the field of the Lords of Death, kill the sleepless serpent guarding the Golden Fleece, and escape with the prize. She also says that she left her father and home and caused Pelias's death for Jason's sake.

l: Aegeus's childlessness, Medea, _Enter from the right_ JASON.
s: Aegeus tells Medea that he is childless because the god has willed it so, and that he has sought an answer from Apollo at Delphi. Medea promises that she knows magical herbs and will make him a father, and this promise helps move him to protect her.

l: love, Medea, _Enter from the right_ JASON.
s: The Chorus describes love as powerful and transitory, capable either of blessing through gentleness or of producing hatred, strife, and destructive desire. It prays that love's good gifts may be separated from its evil ones and that lovers may remain innocent and free from war.

l: exile and homelessness, Medea, _Enter from the right_ JASON.
s: Medea describes exile as being cast out helpless and alone, without a fatherland, home, brother, or city to shelter her. The Chorus likewise laments the fate of a woman driven from her father's home and forced onto a difficult road.

l: Medea, Medea, CHORUS.
s: Medea learns that Aegeus will provide refuge in Athens and decides to feign reconciliation with Jason so that their children can deliver poisoned gifts to the royal bride. Jason accepts Medea’s apparent change of heart and agrees to ask that the children remain in Corinth, while Medea sends them with a robe and golden carcanet. After the royal bride accepts the gifts and the children are spared exile, Medea struggles between her love for them and her determination to hurt Jason, ultimately resolving to kill them. The Chorus laments the children’s threatened deaths, and Medea awaits news of the royal bride’s fate.

l: Medea, Medea, CHORUS.
s: Medea rejoices that Aegeus can give her refuge in Athens and reveals her plan to send poisoned gifts to Jason’s new bride before killing her own children. She pretends to reconcile with Jason, sends the children with the gifts, and later struggles with grief and hesitation before deciding that her children must die.

l: Jason, Medea, CHORUS.
s: Jason answers Medea’s call and accepts her apparent repentance. He praises her wisdom, promises to protect the children, agrees to ask that they remain in Corinth, and allows them to carry gifts to his new bride.

l: the two children of Jason and Medea, Medea, CHORUS.
s: The children greet Jason during Medea’s feigned reconciliation and are told that they have been spared exile. They carry Medea’s robe and golden carcanet to the royal bride, then return to Medea before she sends them back into the house.

l: the Chorus of Corinthian Women, Medea, CHORUS.
s: The Chorus celebrates Athens and Aegeus before Medea reveals her plans, then urges her not to kill the children. It later foresees the royal bride’s death from the gifts and laments the children’s impending fate.

l: Jason's new bride, Medea, CHORUS.
s: The royal bride accepts Medea’s gifts and thereby spares the children from exile. The Chorus foresees that the poisoned robe and crown will kill her.

l: Athens, Medea, CHORUS.
s: Athens is identified by Medea as the walled refuge where she intends to escape after carrying out her plans.

l: Corinth, Medea, CHORUS.
s: Corinth is the place from which Medea is being exiled and where Jason’s new marriage and the royal bride’s household are located. Jason and Medea discuss allowing the children to remain there.

l: the marriage of Jason and Creon's daughter, Medea, CHORUS.
s: Medea pretends that she now accepts Jason’s marriage to a queen and calls the arrangement wise and beneficial. She uses this apparent acceptance to gain access for her revenge.

l: Medea's exile, Medea, CHORUS.
s: Medea agrees to leave Corinth and describes herself as going into exile. She tries to secure permission for the children to remain, while recognizing that she will be separated from them.

l: the killing of the royal bride, Medea, CHORUS.
s: Medea plans to kill the royal bride by sending her a robe and a golden carcanet treated with poison. The Chorus later reports that the bride has accepted the gifts and is doomed.

l: the killing of Medea's children, Medea, CHORUS.
s: Medea repeatedly declares that she will kill her children in order to wound Jason and prevent her enemies from mocking them. She briefly considers abandoning the plan when she sees them, but finally sends them inside and maintains that the killing cannot be escaped.

l: the poison, Medea, CHORUS.
s: Medea intends the poison to be contained in the robe and crown given to the royal bride. She says that the poison will kill the bride and anyone who touches her in her agony.

l: poisoned gifts, Medea, CHORUS.
s: The gifts consist of fine robes and a golden carcanet, which Medea sends through the children to Jason’s bride. Medea says that such gifts can persuade gods and people, while the Chorus identifies them as instruments of the bride’s death.

l: Medea's revenge, Medea, CHORUS.
s: Medea’s revenge is directed against Jason, his new bride, and the household that has caused her exile. She plans to kill the royal bride and the children so that Jason will be left childless and suffer the greatest possible grief.

l: Medea, Medea, [_Enter_ MESSENGER.
s: The Messenger reports that Medea's poisoned gifts have killed the princess and the king. Medea resolves to kill her own children, and does so despite their cries and the Chorus's attempts to stop her. Jason arrives too late, and Medea appears above him in a winged-dragon chariot with the children's bodies, refusing to let him bury them. Medea declares that vengeance for Jason's betrayal has been completed, while Jason is left childless and grieving.

l: Medea, Medea, [_Enter_ MESSENGER.
s: Medea learns from the Messenger that the princess and the king have died and expresses satisfaction. She kills her children to prevent them from falling into the hands of her enemies, then escapes in the winged-dragon chariot and refuses Jason's pleas to touch or bury their bodies.

l: Jason, Medea, [_Enter_ MESSENGER.
s: Jason comes to save his children from the dead king's kinsmen, but learns that Medea has killed them. He curses Medea, grieves that he is childless, and begs to touch and bury the children; Medea refuses him.

l: Messenger, Medea, [_Enter_ MESSENGER.
s: The Messenger warns Medea to flee because the princess and the king have been killed by her poison. He describes how the princess's golden crown and fine robes burned her flesh and how the king died while embracing her.

l: the two children of Jason and Medea, Medea, [_Enter_ MESSENGER.
s: Medea's children bring the poisoned gifts to the princess and later are killed by Medea inside the house. Their bodies are carried with Medea in the winged-dragon chariot, and Jason is denied the chance to touch or bury them.

l: Jason's new bride, Medea, [_Enter_ MESSENGER.
s: The princess receives the robes and golden crown brought by Medea's children. The gifts burn her, and she dies in agony before her father arrives.

l: Theseus, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, HIPPOLYTUS
s: Theseus is identified as Phaedra's husband and the father of Hippolytus. He is away from Trozên during Phaedra's illness, and Aphrodite intends for him to hear a damaging account and use one of the prayers granted him by the Lord of the Main against Hippolytus.

l: Phaedra, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, HIPPOLYTUS
s: Phaedra is brought from the castle in a weakened condition after fasting for three days. She speaks feverishly of springs, mountains, hunting, horses, and Artemis before admitting that she loves Hippolytus and that this love is the source of her grief and shame.

l: Hippolytus, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, HIPPOLYTUS
s: Hippolytus returns from hunting with his huntsmen and praises Artemis. He offers her a garland from a meadow untouched by shepherds or scythe, calls his own life pure, and refuses to honor Aphrodite except from afar.

l: Artemis, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, HIPPOLYTUS
s: Artemis is praised by Hippolytus and the hunters as a holy, virginal goddess and the daughter of Zeus and Leto. Hippolytus seeks to remain devoted to her and follows the hunting life associated with her.

l: the Nurse of Phaedra, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, HIPPOLYTUS
s: The Nurse cares for Phaedra, tries to relieve her physical distress, and repeatedly urges her to reveal the cause of her illness. She finally mentions Hippolytus and draws from Phaedra the confession of her love, then blames Aphrodite for bringing ruin upon Phaedra and the household.

l: the Trozenian women, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, HIPPOLYTUS
s: The Trozenian women gather outside the castle and speculate about the cause of Phaedra's wasting illness. They wonder whether a god, a forgotten sacrifice, Theseus, or news from Crete has caused her suffering, and they question the Nurse about it.

l: Trozên, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, HIPPOLYTUS
s: Trozên is the place where Hippolytus is known for rejecting Aphrodite and where Phaedra and Theseus reside after Theseus's exile. Its women observe Phaedra's illness, and its surrounding mountains, springs, woods, and shore appear in Phaedra's fevered imaginings.

l: the castle, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, HIPPOLYTUS
s: The castle is Theseus's residence in Trozên. Hippolytus and the hunters enter it after the hunt, while Phaedra is brought out from its central door and placed on a couch.

l: Phaedra's love for Hippolytus, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, HIPPOLYTUS
s: Phaedra's love for Hippolytus began when she saw him in Athens during his visit to the Mysteries. Aphrodite caused the love, which has led Phaedra to waste away, fast, and fear that her desire will bring dishonor.

l: purity and innocence, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, HIPPOLYTUS
s: Hippolytus associates purity with a life untouched by ordinary human desire and offers Artemis a garland gathered only by pure hands. Phaedra calls herself clean in hand but questions whether her heart is clean.

l: honor and shame, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, HIPPOLYTUS
s: Phaedra tries to preserve honor by concealing her love, believing that she must build honor out of shame. The Nurse urges her to speak, while Phaedra fears that revealing the truth will disgrace her and her family.

l: illness and suffering, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, HIPPOLYTUS
s: Phaedra's secret love appears as a wasting illness: she lies weak, refuses food, changes restlessly, and speaks in fevered images. The Nurse says that caring for another person's pain is harder than bearing one's own, and the women cannot initially identify the cause.

l: death, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, HIPPOLYTUS
s: Phaedra's fasting and wasting seem likely to lead to death, and she wishes at moments that she could die without thought or knowledge. Aphrodite also foresees death as the outcome of Phaedra's suffering and vengeance against Hippolytus.

l: the gods, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, HIPPOLYTUS
s: The gods are presented as powers whose favor must be respected and whose demands humans must pay. Aphrodite punishes Hippolytus for rejecting her, while Artemis is honored by Hippolytus and invoked by the older woman as a helper in pain.

l: Hippolytus; The Bacchae, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, CHORUS
s: Phaedra explains to the women of Troezen that, after realizing she loved Hippolytus, she tried silence, self-control, and finally resolved to die rather than shame her husband, children, and herself. Phaedra blames the Nurse for betraying her and decides that death is the only remaining way to preserve some honour, while also resolving to bring Hippolytus down with her. l: Phaedra, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, CHORUS

l: the Nurse of Phaedra, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, CHORUS
s: The Nurse argues that Phaedra's love is not extraordinary and that yielding to Cypris is wiser than resisting a divine power. l: Hippolytus, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, CHORUS
s: Hippolytus overhears the Nurse's disclosure and reacts with horror, condemning the Nurse and speaking bitterly against women and Love. He refuses to reveal what he heard only because he had sworn an oath, declares that he will remain silent until Theseus returns, and leaves in fury.

l: the Trozenian women, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, CHORUS
s: The Chorus responds to Phaedra's suffering with sympathy, praises her concern for virtue and honour, and promises not to reveal her secret. It sings of the destructive power of Erôs and Cypris, then mourns Phaedra's fate and foresees her hanging herself in the bridal room.

l: Cypris, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, CHORUS
s: Cypris is described as a powerful goddess whose force brings Love into all life and overwhelms those who resist her. Phaedra sees herself as being murdered by Cypris and decides to let the goddess have her day.

l: Crete, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, CHORUS
s: Phaedra recalls her origins in Crete and refuses to shame the old proud Cretan castle through her conduct. The Chorus refers to the Cretan strand and to Phaedra's voyage from her joyous home to a distant marriage.

l: Trozên, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, CHORUS
s: The Chorus consists of the daughters of Troezen, whom Phaedra addresses while seated at the portal of Pelops' land. Phaedra asks them to keep silent about what they have heard.

l: Love, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, CHORUS

l: honor and shame, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, CHORUS
s: Phaedra insists that honour, rather than comforting false words, must be preserved. She chooses death to avoid dishonouring her husband, children, and family, and seeks to save at least a fragment of honour even after her secret has been exposed.

l: shame, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, CHORUS
s: Phaedra regards both the act and the suffering associated with her forbidden love as shameful. She fears that her shame will be exposed to others and believes that living with it would dishonour her husband, children, and household.

l: death, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, CHORUS
s: Phaedra repeatedly presents death as the best or only remaining response to her love and disgrace. She says that she will die soon, and the Chorus anticipates that her death will come by hanging in the bridal room.

l: Phaedra's suicide by hanging, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, CHORUS
s: Phaedra decides that she will kill herself, though she initially asks how she should die. The Chorus later describes the intended suicide as Phaedra going alone to her bridal room and placing her neck in a noose.

l: Phaedra’s children, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, CHORUS
s: Phaedra says that her children will one day live in ancient Athens as free, honourable men who can be proud of their mother. She fears that her disgrace would shame them and makes their future reputation one reason for choosing death.

l: Hippolytus; The Bacchae, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, THE BACCHAE
s: Dionysus comes to Thebes in human form to establish his worship and vindicate his mother, Semelê. l: Dionysus, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, THE BACCHAE
s: Dionysus arrives in Thebes disguised as a mortal after spreading his dances and rites through Asia and other lands. He plans to establish his worship in Thebes, punish Pentheus for rejecting him, vindicate Semelê, and then continue to another land.

l: Semele, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, THE BACCHAE
s: Semelê is identified as the daughter of Cadmus, the mother of Dionysus, and the bride of Zeus who died when heavenly fire consumed her. Dionysus says he has come to Thebes to preserve her reputation and prove that she truly bore a god.

l: Zeus, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, THE BACCHAE
s: Zeus is identified as the father of Dionysus and the divine partner of Semelê.

l: Cadmus, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, THE BACCHAE
s: Cadmus keeps Semelê's tomb pure and set apart as a sanctuary. He has yielded his throne and royal authority to his daughter's son, Pentheus.

l: Pentheus, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, THE BACCHAE
s: Pentheus is king of Thebes and has begun a war against Dionysus. He rejects Dionysus's worship, refuses him drink-offerings and prayers, and is warned that Dionysus's power will fall upon him and his people.

l: The Bacchae, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, THE BACCHAE
s: The Bacchae are associated with Dionysus's worship, dances, and rites. The text presents the women devoted to him as dwelling in the mountains and following his religious movement.

l: Thebes, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, THE BACCHAE
s: Thebes is the first land in Hellas where Dionysus intends to establish his worship. He says the city will suffer until it recognizes him as a true god.

l: Chorus of Inspired Damsels, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, THE BACCHAE

s: The Eastern Women enter after Dionysus departs, wearing white robes, fawn-skins, and ivy-bound hair and carrying instruments and thyrsi. They begin their mystic song of worship.

l: the Theban women, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, THE BACCHAE
s: Dionysus says that his magic has driven the women of Thebes from their homes, including Cadmus's daughters. They dwell among roofless rocks and green pines on the mountain.

l: Dionysian worship, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, THE BACCHAE
s: Dionysus says he has taught his dances and rites throughout the world and has bound the women to the harness of his rites. He intends to make Thebes recognize and participate in them.

s: Dionysus's birth is attributed to Zeus and Semelê. Semelê's sisters deny this account and claim that she falsely invoked Zeus to conceal human shame, but Dionysus says he has come to prove the truth of his birth.

s: Pentheus's war against Dionysus consists of rejecting Dionysus's person and refusing him drink-offerings and prayers. Dionysus responds by declaring that Pentheus and Thebes will face his power.

l: Hippolytus; The Bacchae, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, CHORUS
s: The Chorus praises Dionysus and describes the ecstatic rites, songs, dances, and mountain worship of his followers. Teiresias and Cadmus, dressed in ivy and fawn-skins, defend the new god, while Pentheus condemns the worship and orders Dionysus's followers and the visiting stranger to be arrested. Teiresias warns Pentheus that his resistance is madness and that Dionysus will become great in Greece. Pentheus rejects their counsel and begins persecuting Dionysus, while the Chorus prays for the god's protection and celebrates the release from care found in wine, dancing, and worship.

l: Dionysus, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, CHORUS
s: Dionysus is praised as the joy-bestower, the god born from Semelê and Zeus, and the lord of ecstatic worship, prophecy, and release from grief. His followers call him Bromios and bring him from the mountains into the streets and towns, while Teiresias predicts that he will become great throughout Greece.

l: Chorus of Inspired Damsels, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, CHORUS
s: The Chorus, composed of Bacchic maidens, sings of Dionysus's birth, powers, rites, and mountain worship. It praises those who honor him, condemns Pentheus's scorn, and prays that divine justice will not destroy the city.

l: Pentheus, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, CHORUS
s: Pentheus hears that Theban women have left their homes for secret rites and orders his guards to capture them and the stranger who teaches the worship of Dionysus. He mocks Teiresias and Cadmus for wearing Bacchic attire, rejects their warnings, and sends men to arrest the stranger and destroy Teiresias's sanctuary.

l: Teiresias, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, CHORUS
s: Teiresias appears dressed for Dionysian worship and joins Cadmus in preparing to dance for the god. He defends Dionysus as a powerful god of wine, prophecy, battle, and spiritual relief, warns Pentheus that his opposition is madness, and leaves with Cadmus to continue their service.

l: Cadmus, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, CHORUS
s: Cadmus comes dressed in ivy and a Bacchic fawn-skin, ready to honor Dionysus despite his age. He urges Pentheus to accept the god, reminds him of Actaeon's destruction for opposing Artemis, and then leaves with Teiresias toward the mountain.

l: the Theban women, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, CHORUS
s: The Theban women, including wives and sisters, are said to have abandoned their homes for secret rites on the hills, where they dance and pray to Dionysus. Pentheus claims that they engage in sexual wrongdoing, but Teiresias argues that the rites need not stain women whose hearts remain pure.

l: Semele, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, CHORUS
s: Semelê is identified as the mother of Dionysus and as the daughter whose death in Zeus's lightning led to the god's unusual birth. The Chorus calls Thebes the nurse of Semelê and urges the city to crown itself with her ivy.

l: Zeus, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, CHORUS
s: Zeus saves the unborn Dionysus from the fire that kills Semelê and devises a secret means for his birth. Teiresias explains that Zeus also protected the child from Hera by giving her a likeness made from a fragment of the world-encircling fire.

l: Thebes, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, CHORUS
s: Thebes is called the nurse of Semelê and is urged to adorn itself with ivy, bryony, oak, and pine in honor of Dionysus. Pentheus's resistance threatens the city, and the Chorus prays that the god will not punish it in anger.

l: mountain wilderness, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, CHORUS
s: The mountain is the place where Dionysian worshippers gather for dancing, prayer, wild revelry, and sacred visions. The Bacchic maidens call for Dionysus to be brought from the mountain, while Pentheus sends his men to hunt the women there.

l: Dionysian worship, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, CHORUS
s: Dionysian worship includes ivy crowns, fawn-skins, thyrsoi, timbrels, pipes, dancing, prayer, sacrifice, wine, and ecstatic movement on the mountains. Teiresias and Cadmus defend it as an ancient and legitimate divine service rather than a source of corruption.

l: the Bacchic procession, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, CHORUS
s: The Bacchic procession is imagined as a joyful movement of maidens from the mountains into streets, towns, and towers, accompanied by timbrels, drums, pipes, Phrygian music, and cries of 'Come, O ye Bacchae.' Its participants follow Dionysus in ecstatic dancing and summon the god into the city.

l: Pentheus's persecution of Dionysus, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, CHORUS
s: Pentheus's persecution begins when he orders the arrest of Dionysian worshippers and commands his guards to seek the girl-faced stranger who has introduced the rites. He also orders Teiresias's sanctuary to be wrecked and threatens the stranger with imprisonment, judgment, and death.

l: forgetting and release from care, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, CHORUS
s: Teiresias says that Dionysus's wine rests the spirit from grieving and allows people to forget the burdens of the day in sleep. The Chorus likewise associates the god with the vanishing of care, the forgiveness of hate, and a crownèd slumber after divine and human feasts.

l: Hippolytus; The Bacchae, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, [_As the Chorus ceases, a party of the guards return, leading in the
s: Dionysus is captured and brought before Pentheus, but he remains calm while Pentheus cuts his hair, takes his wand, and orders him imprisoned. Dionysus escapes when the god shakes Pentheus's Castle with an earthquake and sets fire to Semele's tomb, leaving Pentheus to attack an illusion. A Messenger reports that the wild women, led by Agave, have performed wonders, slaughtered cattle, resisted armed men, and ravaged neighboring villages. Pentheus rejects the warnings and orders his soldiers to assemble against the Bacchae.

l: Dionysus, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, [_As the Chorus ceases, a party of the guards return, leading in the
s: Dionysus is captured, bound, shorn, deprived of his wand, and taken to Pentheus's dungeon. He remains gentle and unafraid, declares that the god will free him, and later escapes when Pentheus attacks an illusion in his likeness. He tells the Chorus that he has come to protect them and that Pentheus's punishment is approaching.

l: Pentheus, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, [_As the Chorus ceases, a party of the guards return, leading in the
s: Pentheus mocks Dionysus's appearance and questioning, rejects Dionysus's god, and orders him bound and imprisoned. After the Castle is shaken and damaged, Pentheus attacks a false image of Dionysus and believes the prisoner has escaped. When the Messenger reports the wild women's deeds, Pentheus orders his armed men to gather and march against them.

l: the Chorus, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, [_As the Chorus ceases, a party of the guards return, leading in the
s: The Chorus laments Dionysus's imprisonment and calls on him to oppose Pentheus. It praises Dionysus as a god and rejoices when the earthquake and fire reveal his power. After Dionysus returns, the Chorus welcomes him and urges Pentheus to honor him.

l: Chorus of Inspired Damsels, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, [_As the Chorus ceases, a party of the guards return, leading in the
s: The imprisoned Maids escape from Pentheus's dungeon without mortal assistance and return to the woods, dancing and rejoicing for Bromios.

l: the Messenger, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, [_As the Chorus ceases, a party of the guards return, leading in the
s: The Messenger returns from Kithaeron and reports that the wild women have performed miraculous acts, slaughtered cattle, defeated armed villagers, and ravaged nearby settlements. He urges Pentheus to accept Dionysus and warns that destroying the god would destroy joy and love.

l: Semele, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, [_As the Chorus ceases, a party of the guards return, leading in the
s: Semele is identified as the mother of Dionysus. The fire from heaven appears upon her tomb when Dionysus summons the god's power.

l: Agave, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, [_As the Chorus ceases, a party of the guards return, leading in the
s: Agave leads one of the three bands of wild women on Kithaeron. She awakens the Bacchae with the god's cry, directs them in worship, and leads them in attacking cattle and ravaging villages.

l: Thebes, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, [_As the Chorus ceases, a party of the guards return, leading in the
s: Thebes is the land where Dionysus seeks to establish his worship and where Pentheus rules. The wild women's actions make Thebes and its surrounding settlements suffer destruction, while Pentheus prepares its forces for war.

l: Kithaeron, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, [_As the Chorus ceases, a party of the guards return, leading in the
s: Kithaeron is the mountain region where the wild women sleep, worship Dionysus, perform wonders, slaughter cattle, and launch attacks on nearby villages.

l: Castle of Pentheus, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, [_As the Chorus ceases, a party of the guards return, leading in the
s: Pentheus's Castle is shaken by a powerful earthquake and struck by fire at Semele's tomb. Its structure is overthrown and left in ruins while Pentheus is inside.

l: the Theban women, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, [_As the Chorus ceases, a party of the guards return, leading in the
s: The wild women sleep in bands on Kithaeron, then awaken to worship Dionysus. They draw water, wine, milk, and honey from the earth, tear apart cattle, defeat armed villagers, carry off children, shatter metal, and ravage nearby settlements without being wounded.

l: thyrsus, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, [_As the Chorus ceases, a party of the guards return, leading in the
s: The thyrsus is Dionysus's wand and is taken from him by Pentheus. In the Messenger's account, the wild women use their wands to bring water from rock, produce wine from the earth, and strike down armed men.

l: Dionysian worship, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, [_As the Chorus ceases, a party of the guards return, leading in the
s: The mysteries of Dionysus are presented as sacred revelations given to his chosen followers. Dionysus says that their emblems and benefits may not be revealed to the uninitiated and that the mysteries reject those who love sin.

l: the earthquake, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, [_As the Chorus ceases, a party of the guards return, leading in the
s: The earthquake is summoned by Dionysus's voice and shakes the pillars of Pentheus's Castle. It accompanies the god's release and the overthrow of Pentheus's house.

l: the fire from heaven, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, [_As the Chorus ceases, a party of the guards return, leading in the
s: The fire from heaven is identified with the blaze that once came upon Semele. It rises from Semele's tomb and burns against Pentheus's house when Dionysus calls upon it.

l: the destruction of Pentheus's house, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, [_As the Chorus ceases, a party of the guards return, leading in the
s: Pentheus's house is destroyed after the earthquake and fire strike it. Dionysus says that the house lies in wreck as a sign of Pentheus's punishment for opposing the god.

l: the slaughter of the cattle, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, [_As the Chorus ceases, a party of the guards return, leading in the
s: The wild women attack the herds on the mountain and tear the cattle apart with their bare hands. Bulls and cows are dismembered, with ribs, limbs, and flesh scattered through the air and among the pine branches.

l: Hippolytus; The Bacchae, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, DIONYSUS
s: Dionysus overcomes Pentheus's resistance and persuades him to spy on the Bacchae while disguised as a woman. Pentheus is dressed in a rich trailing robe, a snood, a dappled fawn-skin, and given a wand; Bacchic madness clouds his judgment. Dionysus leads Pentheus toward Kithaeron and calls on Agave and the Cadmeian sisters to bring about his doom. The Chorus praises freedom from fear, Wisdom, Loveliness, and the enduring strength of the Spirit of God, while calling for Justice and the Wrath of the Lord against Pentheus.

l: Dionysus, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, DIONYSUS
s: Dionysus warns Pentheus not to oppose a god and then manipulates him into agreeing to spy on the Bacchae. He dresses and guides Pentheus toward Kithaeron, declares that Pentheus walks into a doom that will make his name a lasting sign, and invokes Agave and the Cadmeian sisters against him.

l: Pentheus, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, DIONYSUS
s: Pentheus first threatens violence against the Bacchae and resists wearing women's clothing, but Dionysus gradually controls his thoughts and choices. He leaves dressed as a Bacchanal to hide among the pines and observe the Bacchae.

l: Chorus of Inspired Damsels, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, DIONYSUS
s: The Chorus sings of escape into the wilderness, freedom from fear, Wisdom, Loveliness, and the enduring strength of divine law. It calls for Justice and the Wrath of the Lord to punish Pentheus.

l: Bacchae, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, DIONYSUS
s: The Bacchae are described as Dionysus's Chosen, whose mysteries Pentheus seeks to observe. Dionysus says Pentheus will be carried away by them after they discover him.

l: Maenads, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, DIONYSUS
s: The Maenads are portrayed as wild women possessed by God, living on the hills and defending their holy mysteries. The Chorus calls on them to rage against Pentheus, who spies on them in woman's guise.

l: Bacchanals, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, DIONYSUS
s: Pentheus intends to spy upon the Bacchanals and fears that they will triumph over him. He is dressed like one of them before setting out toward the mountain.

l: Agave, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, DIONYSUS
s: Dionysus identifies Pentheus's mother, Agave, as one who will see him and calls on her to reach out her arms for the coming ordeal.

l: Kithaeron, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, DIONYSUS
s: Kithaeron is the mountain region where the Bacchae and their mysteries are found. Pentheus imagines possessing the strength to lift or tear down its steeps and then goes there to hide among the pines.

l: Thebes, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, DIONYSUS
s: Thebes is the city from which Pentheus departs in disguise. In his madness, Pentheus sees Thebes and its Wall of Seven Gates as doubled.

l: mountain wilderness, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, DIONYSUS
s: The mountain is the destination of Pentheus's spying expedition and the setting of the Bacchae's worship. Dionysus leads Pentheus toward it while the Chorus calls for divine judgment there.

l: hills, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, DIONYSUS
s: The hills are described as the place of the Chosen's delight and the Bacchae's worship. Pentheus wants to see the women praying on them.

l: the long dances, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, DIONYSUS
s: The long dances are remembered by the Maidens as dances continuing through the dark until the stars wane. They are associated with dew, wind, running feet, and freedom in the wild lands.

l: Bacchic madness, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, DIONYSUS
s: Bacchic madness overshadows Pentheus after Dionysus dresses him. It clouds his reason, makes him see doubled sights and horns on Dionysus, and fills him with excited, violent, and deluded thoughts.

l: Pentheus's transformation, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, DIONYSUS
s: Pentheus's transformation changes him from a resisting king into a figure dressed as a Bacchanal. He accepts the robe, snood, fawn-skin, and wand, loses power over his own mind, and leaves to spy on the Bacchae.

l: Pentheus's trial, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, DIONYSUS
s: Pentheus's trial is presented as the ordeal awaiting him when he enters the Bacchae's domain. Dionysus says that Pentheus will be carried away and that only God and Dionysus can pass the ordeal unscathed.

l: Pentheus's death, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, DIONYSUS
s: Pentheus's death is foretold but does not occur within this unit. Dionysus says that Pentheus will see the Bacchae and die, and calls his coming doom a lasting sign.

l: the net, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, DIONYSUS
s: Dionysus declares that the lion is walking into the net. The image describes Pentheus entering the trap prepared for him as he goes to spy on the Bacchae.

l: rich trailing robe, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, DIONYSUS
s: Dionysus says Pentheus must wear a rich trailing robe of fine linen for the expedition. The robe becomes part of Pentheus's disguise as a woman.

l: snood, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, DIONYSUS
s: Dionysus places a snood on Pentheus's head as part of his disguise. He later adjusts Pentheus's hair and clothing while Pentheus submits to his care.

l: dappled fawn-skin, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, DIONYSUS
s: The dappled fawn-skin is one of the items Dionysus prescribes for Pentheus's disguise. Pentheus accepts the costume despite his earlier refusal to wear a woman's robe.

l: thyrsus, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, DIONYSUS
s: Dionysus gives Pentheus a wand and instructs him to swing it in his right hand in time with his right foot. Pentheus asks how to carry it so that he will resemble the Bacchae.

l: Wisdom, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, DIONYSUS
s: Wisdom is presented as freedom from fear, the ability to breathe and wait, and the refusal to answer hatred with hatred. The Chorus asks what else Wisdom can be besides this release from striving.

l: Law, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, DIONYSUS
s: The Chorus describes an abiding law that is not made by human striving and that remains strong through the ages. It condemns Pentheus for acting in defiance of such law.

l: Justice, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, DIONYSUS
s: The Chorus summons Justice to appear with a lifted sword against Pentheus. Justice is linked with the punishment of his tyrannous, lawless, and Godless conduct.
